speechtext:
In consequence of a telegram received today, I desire to ask several questions of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) in regard to the single unemployed situation in Vancouver.
1.	Have the departmental representatives been in direct negotiation with the representatives of the single unemployed to discover some basis of settlement of their grievances?

3. Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour):	The hon. member gave
me notice that he intended to ask this question to-day, but I received the questions in the form in which he has presented them only a few minutes before 'three o'clock. I shall deal with them, therefore, on the basis of such information as I have.
The answer to the first question is that thfe representative of the Department of Labour who has been in Vancouver for some time past has been in consultation with the provincial government but has not been in direct negotiation with the representatives of the single unemployed.
In reply to the second question, according to our information the last of the deferred pay vouchers were redeemable on May 15. I am not able to give the exact amount of money due to individuals, owing to the fact that the amount would depend upon the length of time they passed in the camps.
In answer to the third question, I may say the provincial government did undertake the registration of all single unemployed men
who passed through the forestry conservation camps. It was on the basis of that registration that the minister of labour of British Columbia made his proposal that these men who came to British Columbia from other provinces should be returned to their homes in such other provinces. As to work that may be available for those who entered British Columbia from other provinces, I can only say that these men when they return to their homes will be eligible in the same way as others in the same position with respect to youth training plans and such works projects as may be in progress within the provinces to which they go.

speechtext:
I have looked over the record of the last ten years as to the sitting of the house on the king's birthday. In four of the past ten years parliament was not in session. In two of the ten years the house observed the holiday by not sitting. In two others the house adjourned for some time during the day. In 1929 we were having morning sittings at that time and the house adjourned at one o'clock. In 1935 the house adjourned from three-thirty to eight o'clock. In 1936 parliament prorogued on the king's birthday, at five o'clock in the afternoon.
The government would be willing to ascertain what the feeling of the house is with regard to this matter, and I think there would be no better way than to instruct the whips to confer together and report. We shall be quite willing to meet the wishes of the house.

speechtext:
This is the point about which I am concerned, and I am sure other hon. members are concerned about it as well. In the consideration of this bill or any of its sister bills, if I might use that term, we are dealing with the policy of the government in regard to the whole unemployment problem. I have no desire to object in so far as this particular bill is concerned, as far as it goes, to a very limited degree, in dealing with the question of unemployment. It will be recalled that during the discussion of the resolution it was also repeatedly emphasized by the minister, I think, and others, that the very essence of this measure was the question of unemployment, that it dealt with unemployment. Therefore I think it is competent for a member, while approving of this bill, at the same time to call in question the adequacy of this or any other measures I have seen so far to deal properly with the question of unemployment.
I notice that this bill provides for
830,000,000 to be loaned to municipalities for works which are described as self-liquidating projects. While one is naturally inclined to give approval to the move, still one is reminded somewhat of the policy of what are known as small loan companies. There are certain needy borrowers, and these companies hold themselves out as domestic physicians, qualified to deal with domestic problems. They invite the borrowers to come and consult them in regard to the solution of their domestic difficulties; then they lend them money at two per cent per month. Here the federal government, knowing the distress of the municipalities; knowing the domestic
Municipal Improvements

problem, if I might apply that term, that exists in Canada with regard to the financing of the municipalities, says to the municipalities, " Now, we will lend you a certain limited amount of money." In some instances it will be a matter of only a few thousand dollars; in the larger cities it will amount to half a million or more, according to size. But the government says, " You must bring to us first a security that is absolutely self-liquidating and satisfactory to us. Then you must have your note endorsed by the province; and if you comply with these requirements we will lend you the money at two per cent- two per cent per annum."
Well, Mr. Speaker, whatever else may be said about it, certainly this is not a very great contribution towards either the solution of unemployment or the relief of the municipalities from the financial distress under which they are now labouring. During the debate on this general subject some weeks ago-I am not permitted to quote it, but I think there can be no objection to my just referring to it- I took the liberty of pointing out to the house that one of the chief problems in Canada was that municipalities-the same thing applies to provinces, but for the moment I am limiting myself to municipalities-are called upon to bear new burdens in these days, peculiar to the conditions that have existed for the last eight, nine or ten years. They are called upon to bear new and onerous burdens; that is, to pay a substantial share of the cost of general unemployment relief, and, incidentally, to care for ever-increasing numbers of indigent people; because without question the numbers of indigents to-day have increased greatly as compared to the numbers for whom the municipalities were called upon to care a few years ago. That of course is altogether apart from what one might call industrial unemployment.
This bill offers no relief to the municipalities in that regard at all; I think one would search in vain through the measures presented to the house to find any suggestion of giving assistance to the municipalities in that way or for that purpose. I believe it would have been infinitely better at this time had the government provided $30,000,000 or more to, shall I use the word, subsidize the municipalities, to assist them in carrying on their burden of finance in these days of ever-increasing social duties. I know that immediately the answer will be made that this parliament cannot vote money to municipalities, because municipalities are the creature of the provinces. All that is admitted, but I

do submit that where there is a will to achieve an end, ways and means to reach that end can always be found.
What are the municipalities faced with, and what is the effect generally on the country of their condition? In the first place, they have increased taxes upon realty to a point where it is admitted by all that new building operations are virtually an impossibility because of the heavy burden of the realty tax. We are told that another bill will foe introduced, dealing with housing. But at the very root of the housing problem lies the weight of municipal or city taxation, and it is not wholly the fault of the municipality. I will admit that during the years of industrial activity and prosperity, many cities and municipalities were somewhat reckless in their borrowing. But that was not peculiar to municipalities; it was common to them, to provincial governments and to the dominion government; and furthermore it was prevalent in private industrial corporations. All through the economic structure in the days of activity we had a degree of profligacy, if you like to use that extreme term, or recklessness in borrowing which we now realize was improvident and unwise. It does not lie within the right of this parliament to reflect upon the municipalities for having been improvident in the past, because the whole country is at fault in that respect. The failure to move forward in necessary construction is fundamentally due to the heavy taxation on realty in the municipalities. A month ago or more I made the suggestion that parliament might consider subsidizing municipalities to effect a reduction in taxation, in other words, offer to assist them by grants if a corresponding reduction were made in the rate of taxation on realty in the cities. If something of that kind were done-and I submit it would not cost this year more than this amount of $30,000,000-it would be infinitely more effective in starting the wheels of industry through a building program than will the rather left-handed method of assistance suggested in this bill. That is one point I wish to emphasize.
The other point is this question of unemployed single men. What are we going to do about it? Apparently, as near as I can judge, we are going to do nothing more about it than is set forth in the supplementary estimates tabled a week or two ago. In these estimates I see very little for that purpose. There are some other grants in aid to the provinces, but these grants in all probability will-

speechtext:
I did not say anything on the resolution which preceded this bill, not because I did not feel there was something which could be said, but because I was and am in agreement with the proposals in the bill. I have no doubt that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) realizes just as much as the rest of us that the bill is not perfect or adequate to meet the situation now confronting the people of Canada. However, in my opinion the bill is a good start. The principle involved is a good one. I disagree with the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens); I believe that this method of providing funds for the municipalities is much better than to grant subsidies. The time may come when that will be necessary, but for the present I believe that this is the better way of dealing with the problem. It is unfortunate, but the fact is that when a municipality receives money, through either federal or provincial agencies, it considers it as something that has

Municipal Improvements

come right out of the sky and that may be spent without any great regard for economic consequences. I have seen that happen time and time again. As I say, the time may come when this government will have to help the municipalities, through subsidies, but if that is done there will have to be very stringent control over the expenditure of the money.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS

I disagree again with the hon. member for Kootenay East. I am doubtful of its being possible to reduce taxation in that way. I came here in 1930 when we were just entering the depression. At the special session of 1930 the government decided to appropriate S20,000.000 to meet the unemployment conditions of that time, with which action I agreed. The intentions were good, but I am convinced now that that $20,000,000 did more harm than good. Some municipalities actually went into bankruptcy in order to meet the dollar for dollar provision.
I do not wish to say anything more about this bill. If this session lasts much longer I am sure the government will have to consider other measures to meet the situation that now confronts us. The fact that home building is at a low ebb is not due altogether to high taxation. The poor are without homes, but we must realize that they are also without clothing and without proper food. High taxation does not prevent their getting new clothes. High taxation does not prevent their getting proper food. Some little time ago I attended a meeting where this housing question was being discussed. One gentleman said that the reason why the housing situation was so bad was that the building trades were organized so well and had forced up wages to a point where people were not able to build because of the increased cost. When I heard that statement I thought of the report of the textile commission. No one can say that wages are high in the textile industry. No one can say that wages are high in the clothing industry. No one can say that wages are high in the boot and shoe industry. No one can say that the prices received by the farmers for their farm products are too high. Yet the workers need clothes, they need boots and shoes and they need decent food. The high wages paid in the building or any other industry is not the cause of the poverty of the working class.
Let me repeat that I approve of this measure, but I believe that a great deal will depend

upon the way it is administered. I have already brought it to the attention of the authorities in Vancouver and I hope they will be able to take advantage of it so far as it goes.

Now I come back to this, and I cannot stress it too strongly. Can any hon. member of this house visualize the circumstances under which the government introduces at the end of May a bill that contemplates these acts being done, involving action by legislatures, and seeing the legislatures come and go, without this government taking any steps? Is this policy a new policy? Was it thought out before the house met? Was it thought out when the legislatures were in session? Was it considered whether they were in session or not? Is it any wonder that the people of this country ask, what is the matter with parliament? Why is no action being taken, they ask, to deal with the unemployment problem? There are inquiries and correspondence everywhere, asking why nothing is being done. And then when the mountain labours and brings forth a mouse, what have we? We are told that what the government is doing is part of a grand policy to deal with unemployment. The Minister of Labour said: Keep that in mind- this is only part of a program. How long have they had the program? How long have they had the policy? Did they have it when the legislature of Prince Edward Island was in session, or the legislature of Alberta, or of British Columbia, or of Quebec, or Ontario? If they had, why didn't they act? If they had not, why did they not bring down a policy that does not contemplate the necessity of the legislatures meeting in special session?
With respect to the meeting of the legislatures the minister used these words, at page 3399 of Hansard:
Perhaps I should at this stage indicate what is in the mind of the government regarding the point raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). In fact, I think I should apologize for not having anticipated it, but I overlooked it completely in making my statement.
The laws of the provinces relating to municipal expenditures vary very widely; the powers vested by the legislatures in the various lieutenant governors in council vary very widely as also do the powers extended to municipalities to do certain things involving capital expenditure. It is quite impossible to frame a measure which would meet all the varying conditions, and I was compelled therefore to visualize the possibility that this scheme might have a sufficient appeal to the various provincial authorities to warrant them even in calling the legislature together for a couple of days to make possible what might be required in their particular case, for the
municipalities on the one hand and for themselves on the other, to enable them to come within the ambit of the legislation.
I will be perfectly frank, Mr. Chairman, and say that I do not think the dominion can extend this credit on any less secured terms than those involved in the bill. As the one charged with the guardianship of the treasury, I should say that I believe the security asked for by this legislation is reasonable and no more adequate so far as the dominion is concerned, especially when we have in mind the fact that each legislature controls absolutely the municipalities within its borders. The municipalities are wholly the creatures at all times of the provincial legislatures. If we proceed to lend direct to the municipalities- and there is some question whether we could, as indicated by the leader of the opposition-it would be open to any provincial legislature so to change the conditions under which its municipalities operate as to make it quite impossible for us to get the money back. We might as well face that. That being the case, seeing that we are rendering this assistance to institutions which are wholly the creatures of provincial legislatures, I think that when we are lending the money so cheaply, when we are taking the degree of loss on the loan which I indicated in my earlier remarks on the subject, the minimum security we should ask is that the province should guarantee that the municipality will keep the obligation it has incurred for a project; and remember, that the project must itself have the approval of the provincial government before it can become eligible for a loan under this statute.
I have read the whole passage in order that there may be no difficulty on that score, and I do point out that nothing short of a provincial statute will meet the conditions imposed in some provinces. Obviously, I cannot speak for all of them, but I say that some of them require an act of the provincial legislature; and what is more, sir, the minister himself recognizes it. He said he thought that they might meet together for two days- it is important enough for that-in special session to deal with the matter. And they allowed the legislatures to meet and prorogue, while they did nothing. That is the policy, that is the program of the government. Do you call that a policy, Mr. Speaker? Do you call that a program? What do you think the Canadian people would have felt like if they had been told in 1935, "Our program is to call parliament together in January and let the months of February, March, April and May go by, and in the closing days of May put a resolution on the order paper, following that up with a bill, the second reading of that bill being moved on the second day of June, contemplating at the same time, both in the resolution and in the bill, that nothing short of an act of the legislature, in some of the provinces at any rate, would comply with the terms of that program or policy." For the Minister of Finance himself, speaking for the government,

so intimated. But it does not apply to this alone. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) the other day said, "There is other legislation and the same principle is to be applied." Housing was one matter which was mentioned.
Some day, Mr. Speaker, I will read a few extracts from Hansard of 1934 and 1935, when action was being taken in March, when we called together the provincial premiers and obtained their views as to what had to be done. I am bound to say that I never found any difficulty in dealing with them except in one instance. They pressed their views, and we reached agreements which were loyally carried out by the provinces on the one hand and by the dominion on the other; and if there were differences of opinion they were liquidated peacefully and quietly. But in 1935 the placards declared that there was to be, "Harmony! harmony! There are eight provinces, and we shall have the nine of them wtih the dominion, all one happy family of Liberalism." That was what was broadcast to the electors of the country, and now we have the full fruition of it in a bill that can be made effective in 1938 only in some parts of Canada by an act of the legislature which would involve that body meeting in special 'session, as pointed out by the Minister of Finance. That is the story. And, what is more, as pointed out in the communications that I have been receiving, these contracts and arrangements should all have been made before June; in other words, the time to prepare for them was during the months that have passed. I see no harm in subsidizing the municipalities as a means of improving their public utilities and services; but as a serious means of solving unemployment I do not think this bill can be expected to work very effectively.
In my opinion this bill indicates a tendency on the part of the government to indulge in a mild form of what has come to be known in the United States as pumppriming, which has not solved the unemployment problem in that country and will not solve the unemployment problem in Canada. I do not wish to discuss unemployment now, except to say that it is a world-wide condition, and I believe it is here to stay. But the right of the people to live should have precedence over any man-made rules and regulations, and until some government, this or some other, accepts those two facts and correlates them to our outworn money system, the effect of unemployment will grow and grow'. I do not do this with any desire of declining to give further consideration to his suggestions. Here is the first difficulty with respect to the joint boards. We have had to place a limitation upon the amount which any one municipality can get. This limitation is based upon the relation of its population to the population of Canada. It would be possible to have a joint board made up of one large municipality and several small ones. If each municipality deals separately with the minister with respect to some self-liquidating project, the small municipalities, in spite of not .having sufficient population, could borrow up to $200,000. The large municipality would be subject to the limitation which works out at about $3 per head. The difficulty of adjusting a joint project to what I know the individual municipalities will want to do, that is, take advantage of what they would be entitled to, will in practice be
overcome in the case of most joint water boards by the fact that the individual municipality cooperating in a joint waterworks undertaking almost invariably builds its own laterals within its own borders. That is to say, the joint water board exists for the purpose of delivering water to the boundary of the municipality, or to some agreed-upon point. The development of the distributing system would in many cases offer opportunity to the municipality to take advantage of this scheme. This would be particularly true in connection with the repair and renewal necessities of old lateral distributing systems. I know of many cases where old wooden stave pipes are being used at a tremendous maintenance cost. It has been demonstrated to me that in some cases the maintenance cost considerably exceeds the two per cent interest and carrying charges on these loans. This is the type of work that would create employment.

speechtext: But "on the basis of conservative estimates" would over the period-

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I hope it will continue that way in Calgary. At any rate this is a subject of some difficulty.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: The matter referred to by the right hon. gentleman gives rise to a question I should like to ask. In the city of Windsor the street railway is operated by the hydro-electric commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Owned by?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: It is owned by the city, but there is some scheme of operation which has been entered into 'between the city and the local hydro-electric commission. I should like to know if the present system could be expanded or a substitute bus system brought into being under subsection (c) of section 2. Would that be considered a self-liquidating project?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: To ask me to describe what is a self-liquidating project without critical examination of what is involved is more than I can do. I find it difficult to think of a municipality attempting to develop transportation under the auspices of a scheme of this sort. I would not definitely debar it, but the self-liquidating project that we have in mind is in connection with facilities generally in use by a municipality. Exceptional cases, such as the one mentioned by my hon. friend, and the case of Calgary, referred to by the leader of the opposition, would have to be studied. I may state frankly to. the committee that I am not anxious to widen the definition of "self-liquidating works." I do not want to be put in the position of being accused of agreeing to lend to this municipality and not agreeing to lend to that municipality. I should like to have one rule that will be generally applied. I fear that to widen the definition would add very materially to my responsibility.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I agree with what the minister says about desiring to keep this within bounds, but I should like to have his reaction to this picture. A certain municipality at the present time is circumscribed by Indian reserve lands. It is tending to outgrow its present boundaries and unquestionably it will come before the Indian department to ask for permission to purchase certain of these reserve lands. In doing so it will add to its area and increase its taxes. Would that picture come within the provisions of this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Absolutely not. I can answer that quite positively. The purchase of land is not a work creating project.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Taxes would develop immediately by the purchase of these lands. I just wanted to be clear about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: My hon. friend is very persuasive, but I am quite sure that such a project would not come within the requirements of the bill. It would not have the effect of creating employment.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: How about a sewage system?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: If they borrowed for that purpose, that might be conceivable.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
I see that paragraph (b) of section 2 defines "municipality" as including:
-a city, town, incorporated village, county, township, rural municipality, local improvement district or a province where such province is administering directly territory not organized into county or municipal units.

Municipal Improvements
Irrigation projects have not yet been mentioned in the discussion, and I was thinking of the possibility of irrigation projects being undertaken on the prairie. I have one in mind which would be larger perhaps than would be allowed under the bill, but would an irrigation project be considered by the minister, who is a westerner, as self-liquidating?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: It would depend somewhat on the financial set-up proposed for the irrigation district. As my hon. friend knows, there have been many irrigation projects which have not been self-liquidating by any means. I think, however, that an irrigation project oould scarcely come within the purview of this legislation for another reason. The limitations imposed in the matter of population as to the amount which could be secured would scarcely, I think, make possible an irrigation scheme of any size under this act.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Reverting to sewerage systems, the bill requires the scheme to be self-liquidating. AVould' the minister regard a scheme as coming within the terms of the bill if the municipality put on a special rate to cover the interest charges? Usually there is no charge for the use of the sewerage system. It is general to the municipality. But suppose a municipality undertook to earmark a mill rate sufficient to meet the interest charges per year, would that be regarded as self-liquidating?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: No. The object of the bill is not to encourage municipalities to add to their general municipal rate. Sewerage systems that are built on a service charge basis, whereby those benefiting from the sewerage extension over a period of years pay for it, would be within the purview of the bill as being self-liquidating, but not a project proposed to be dealt with by the imposition of an additional mill rate on the whole municipality through the medium of the general tax. That would not be self-liquidating.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I suggested a mill rate specially earmarked for the project.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
I shall be glad to look into it, but I do not think it would be within the purview of the bill because it would have the effect of increasing the general rate of the municipality. If my hon. friend will study the language of paragraph (c) he will see that it says:
"Self-liquidating projects" means a project which when completed will .	.	. either by
reductions in the annual operating and maintenance charges . . . or by increase of revenues from persons using the services of or otherwise benefiting from the project-
And so on.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
I should like to call
the minister's attention to the wording of paragraphs (b) and (c), having in mind that in Ontario, at all events, in a good many municipalities waterworks and electric light systems are handled by a public utility commission. A public utility commission is an incorporated body, but when it comes to raising money for the purposes of the utility, that I think is up to the municipality as such. The revenues, I think I am correct in saying, go to the public utility body, which at a later date, when they have no further need of them, turns them over to the municipality. It occurs to me that in order to take care of that situation the wording of paragraph (c) might require to be slightly revised, since it does not necessarily mean an increase in the annual net revenue of the municipality. Some provision perhaps should be made to take care of cases where the public utility body receives the revenues from an extension of the water service or something of that kind, and turns over the surplus revenues from time to time to the municipality.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
But surely the annual
revenue of such a public utility body is calculated to be sufficient to take care of the debt charges created by the utility. Surely it must pay over annually to the municipality an amount sufficient to take care of the carrying charges. As far as I am familiar with public utility commissions, they are put in the relationship to the municipality generally of having to contribute to the general treasury an amount equivalent to the carrying charges on the utility which they are administering; but they may hold in reserve, as a branch of municipal government, their earnings over and above those fixed charges. In any case I do not anticipate any difficulty in working that out. From a conservative estimate-not a political conservative estimate. but an economic conservative estimate -of what we can expect over a period of years with respect to the utility, I do not anticipate any difficulty such as my hon. friend mentions. The difficulty would come in connection with boards that have to deal with several municipalities.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
The answer of the hon.
minister to the member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) leaves me with considerable confusion in my mind as to a kind of project in respect of which I think the minister will receive many applications from Ontario. In order to illustrate clearly the one which I wish to know about, in view of this definition, I will mention very briefly one which I
Municipal Improvements

think would clearly come within it. Suppose the municipality desires to construct a waterworks system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: To construct one?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: To construct a waterworks system. Ordinarily a municipality in Ontario charges each user of the water either a flat rate per month or on the basis of a water meter, a gallonage basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
Or on the basis of a
frontage tax.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
That is possible, but not
usual in Ontario in respect of water systems. I assume that that would be a self-liquidating project.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Clearly.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: But now I want to mention a project that is very different and ask for the minister's interpretation. Assume that a municipality wants to instal a sewer and sewerage system. In that case there is no monthly rendering of accounts and no monthly payment by the user, but in lieu thereof a proportion of the cost of the construction of the sewers and the sewerage disposal works is assessed per foot frontage against the property benefited, and there is taken into the general rate of the municipality that portion of the cost which is represented where the sewers have to cross streets at intersections. Would a scheme of that kind be considered self-liquidating, bearing in mind that the cost thereof is specially assessed against the property owner and included in the tax bill along with the general rate, and payable over the term of years which the engineer estimates to be the life of the work?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I attempted to meet that, as will be clear later on in the bill, by making provision for paying part of the cost out of the proceeds of a loan under this bill. What I visualized was this, that the part of the cost of the sewerage system cited by my hon. friend-*

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Specially assessed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
-which is specially assessed could be financed under this scheme. The rest of it the municipality generally would have to take care of. But I would not like to be too definite in saying yes to specific cases that are put to me across the floor. My hon. friend understands that I am not now saying that municipality so-and-so can come along and get a loan. The class of cases I contemplated when framing the bill did include the possibility of a portion of a facility being on a basis which would come
[Mr. Lawson.1
within the purview of the act, and another portion of the same facility being on a different basis; and in order to make possible the consideration of assisting any such work " partly " was put in.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS

There would be no
difference to the security.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
In which event the
municipality in the ordinary course of events would issue debentures for payment for the very work we have been discussing, and I assume that the government would take from the municipality a proportion of those debentures to secure the amount advanced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I wish to point this out to the minister-and he will bear in mind that when I asked the original question I wanted to know what the government had in contemplation; that was all. If I understood his statement a few minutes ago, in answer to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill)-and that is what prompted me to ask the question-the minister said that the government would not favour under this scheme works that imposed additional taxation upon the municipal property or home owner.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: The general municipal rate.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: We have no objection to that.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
There are two questions which I should like to ask the minister. When any municipality desires to extend its sewage system or its waterworks, will that municipality be able to borrow under this bill for that purpose?

Municipal Improvements

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: It would depend upon whether it was self-liquidating.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: If it were specially assessed I presume it would be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: If it were specially assessed on those whom it benefited, yes.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: The other question is this: If a town or a city desires to hard-surface its main street, will it be possible for that town or city to borrow money under this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Again, if it were a self-liquidating project which conceivably might occur in such a case partly in one way and partly in another. Assume that the present street is all broken up and requires a very heavy expense of maintenance year by year, an expense of which there is record which is ascertainable. Assume further that the cost cf the paving is to be assessed on a frontage basis against the property on either side. The combination of those two factors, (1) a lowering of maintenance costs as a result of the work and (2), the assessing of the cost of it on those benefiting, might very well bring such a project within the terms of the act. But remember again, I repeat, I do not want to give specific assurances which will be taken to mean that anyone can come along and ask for a loan to pave a street. It must be demonstrated that the particular project does fall within the definition of self-liquidating public work.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I wish to thank the minister for his reply. I have in mind a special case, and his answer is really encouraging.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Reference has been made to self-liquidating projects where a municipal levy may be used for waterworks or sewage disposal undertakings. What will happen with respect to applications made for repairing school houses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I had not contemplated that.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I think it had better be contemplated. Do I understand that the minister is definitely ruling that feature out of this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I am not ruling out anything which can be demonstrated to the government to be self-liquidating within the language of the statute. It must be self-liquidating.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
I appreciate what the minister has said with regard to the self-liquidating aspect of this matter. May I briefly recite for his information a case that is
now before the Department of Transport in connection with the Niagara peninsula. I am referring to a very definite sewage disposal scheme which is necessary in consequence of a condition that has been brought to the attention of the municipality by the department of health of the province of Ontario. In the hands of the engineers of the Department of Transport there is now the report that has been prepared in conjunction with the department for an extensive sewage disposal scheme which is to take in a group of municipalities. It has been brought about quite definitely by representations from the department of health in Toronto, who object to the raw sewage and industrial waste emptying into lake Ontario. If these municipalities collectively enter into some scheme of providing a trunk sewer that will take care of all this industrial waste and sewage, treated to an extent probably approved by the provincial government, will the minister go so far as to suggest that, by reason of the fact that the federal government is more or less involved in consequence of certain conditions that have grown up over a long period of years in connection with the establishment of industries and so on, consideration could be given to a large joint scheme such as this, undertaken by the municipalities? Would it be possible to assist them in advancing such a scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: From the manner in which my hon. friend sets it out I doubt very much whether it could be arranged. Of course, no one can tell until the actual concrete proposition is submitted. When that is done one will look at the actual proposition and ask whether it is a project which, when completed, will on the basis of conservative estimates result in an increase in annual net revenue to the municipality either by saving money or by a service charge on those benefiting. I am sorry I cannot give a categorical answer, because my hon. friend is outlining something which is still in embryo. Let me say, however, that he must not forget that the degree of financial assistance which would be possible for qualified projects is limited by the populations affected. What would be the population in the municipalities to which my hon. friend is referring?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: About 50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Well, the maximum loan that they could get even with a qualified project would be $200,000.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
For each municipality or
for all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
That is a question which, as I have pointed out, is giving me some
Municipal Improvements

difficulty. Certainly it is difficult for me to see how five municipalities can call themselves five separate entities and get the maximum for small municipalities, when they have by their own action made themselves into a large municipality. It is very difficult for me to answer. Certainly, if they deal with self-liquidating projects of their own individually, they could go up to $200,000. But to say that by merging their populations they are still able to take the advantage which accrues only to those of small populations is a doubtful thing for me to promise at this stage.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Why should there be such a provision in the bill? I intended raising that point on. another section.. There should be some flexibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend mind leaving that until we reach that section? We might let section 2 stand. I think I have all the suggestions I am likely to get on the definition of the term "self-liquidating." They will all be carefully considered.
Section 2 stands.
On section 3-Loans to municipalities.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
In the words of another, I should like to make a few observations. Perhaps this bill is late in coming. But it is better late than never. Jacob-I mean the first Jacob-waited fourteen years for Rachel, and Jacob thought she was worth waiting for. I would say that this bill was well worth waiting for.
I took considerable interest in the convention held some time ago of mayors and aldermen of the cities of Canada. They made some great speeches, speeches which I suppose would compare favourably with the oratory in this house, in demanding something from the dominion. I say this bill is something. It may not be a great deal, but it is something. It is now up to the civic officials to show their business ability. Let me give a concrete example of what a man was able to do with S30. He is the Reverend Richmond Craig of Winnipeg. He began with $30 and a heap of junk and rubbish; he gave a man a meal for sorting this heap, and with his business brain-I think ministers compare favourably with mayors in business ability- he organized a business employing the down-and-outs of Winnipeg. Hon. members from Winnipeg will bear me out. He set them to mending old boots and shoes, clothes, beds, clocks, stoves, etc. He paid the minimum wage to men who could not get a job anywhere else and were down and out. In 1933 his payroll amounted to $13,000. In 1937 the

Good Will Industries showed interesting growth; during a period of six years the sum of $150,000 was paid out in wages, the minimum wage being paid, and a six storey building is now occupied. This shows what an ordinary individual could do. Why cannot our mayors and civic authorities borrow some of this money at two per cent and make it live? Why cannot they use it, not for something that will start and stop never to go again, but for something that will keep going and make work. I do not mean sewers and electric light plants. Let them use their business ability to find something that will be a going concern. I commend the minister for this step; it is only a small thing yet, but it is bound to grow.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: This clause brings us back to the scheme I suggested. It includes waterworks, etcetera. The minister probably did not understand that the project I have in mind is proposed by a group of municipalities which will act independently.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: They will act separately?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: They will have to act separately. Let me be more explicit. The project starts at the outlet of the Welland ship canal; the old basin is being polluted, and the municipalities of St. Catharines, Port Dalhousie, Merritton and Thorold, all separate municipalities, are now considering this large scheme of treating their sewage and industrial waste. They will have to act separately, but they have had a joint meeting-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: To coordinate?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: -to coordinate their interests. It seems to me it should be possible-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Provided it is selfliquidating.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
That is the point I am coming to. This will replace some of the old trunk sewers of these several municipalities. They have to replace them; the provincial government says they must be replaced, that this condition must be cured in some way. Each municipality will have to assume part of the cost of this main trunk sewer which is to carry the sewage in a treated condition into lake Ontario. The present system is on a basis of contributions by each one that uses it. I wished to get some direction as to whether in such a scheme as I have outlined a group of municipalities could come under the provisions of this bill by coordinating their interests.

M unicipal Improvements

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: We are not concerned about whether a municipality coordinates a self-liquidating project with one of another municipality; if within each of the municipalities concerned it can be demonstrated that such a project as my hon. friend outlines will be self-liquidating within the language of the section, it will qualify. Otherwise it may be possible, as mentioned by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson), that parts of the project might be self-liquidating within the definition and other parts not. That would not, in my opinion, bar the municipality from taking advantage of this scheme for the parts that are self-liquidating. It is difficult to deal positively with a hypothetical case; I cannot speak positively about it.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: On many occasions when requests for public expenditures were made the minister asked hon. members where the money would come from. Would he explain to the committee how the money is to be raised for the expenditure involved in this bill? Does he intend going on the open market to raise the money, or to follow the precedent adopted by the government of 1934, which expended a large sum for public works and printed new currency for it? I am not pretending to be an expert on money, but I am tempted to ask the question because of the success which apparently attended the experiment tried in 1934. I think the government still have power to issue a certain amount of currency, and if that could be done, instead of showing a deficit on the proposed scheme, I think they would actually have a profit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon. friend cannot, on a bill of this kind, get an answer to a question on monetary policy. I would call his attention to the first words
of the section now under discussion:
The minister . . . may enter into an agreement with any municipality to make a loan or loans to such municipality out of any unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund. . . .
That is the authority conferred upon the minister by this bill. I cannot indicate the manner in which the consolidated revenue fund will be replenished. I cannot indicate that there will be any change in the methods followed hitherto by the present government to replenish the consolidated revenue fund. Perhaps if my hon. friend would read my remarks of the other day with respect to the cost of this scheme to the government, he would see that there I contemplated the payment of interest upon the money by the dominion government, and that is the basis of the calculations.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: That is why I said the government might have made a profit instead of showing a loss, as was stated by the' minister, because I had in mind the remarks of the minister the other day when he introduced the resolution. Is there really any objection on the part of the government to issuing new currency, as was done in 1934?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I certainly will not go into a discussion of major monetary policy, Mr. Chairman, nor do I think my hon. friend really expects me to do so. He is asking what might be called a general question without expecting me to say that it would be beneficial or otherwise to Canada for so much more-so much more-or so much more than that-of money to be printed and used for this purpose. I do not feel inclined to go into a discussion of that. The management of credit and currency in the country through the central bank is being conducted on scientific lines with the best interests of the whole economy in view. A few weeks ago I indicated the manner in which that had been conducted so far, the expansion that took place in the credit base, and the general reasons underlying it. I do not think my hon. friend would expect me to go further.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: It was done in 1934; a precedent was established then, and on that occasion I think it worked out fairly satisfactorily. All the harm that was predicted did not come about, and without knowing a great deal about the subject I still have a feeling that if the principle were extended a little on this occasion the same good results might be obtained.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
I was quite enthusiastic in connection with the former housing act, which contemplated that the municipalities would participate as lending authorities. Many of them were keen to do so, but an obstacle arose through the fact that there was no possibility of transactions taking place as between the municipal government and the federal government. At the last meet-irg of the union of municipalities of British Columbia a proposal was presented to have the municipal act amended to permit such transactions; but the union of municipalities had in mind the unfortunate financial position of some of the smaller municipalities, and refused to act upon the resolution.
I should like to ask in a general way what course is to be pursued by a municipality which desires to construct a complete sewerage system. It cannot do business directly with the federal government and under this act it

Municipal Improvements

must have the approval and guarantee of the provincial government. That municipality must have an outlet for its sewerage. In the case to which I refer the only outlet is the Columbia river, some five or six miles distant. Between the first municipality, serving about five thousand people, and the next municipality, serving about eleven thousand people, there is a district containing three or four thousand people, and there must be a trunk sewer. Some of it would be in organized municipalities, and a proportion would be in a provincial district. The question is who applies for the loan? Certainly the main portion of the trunk sewer, serving the municipalities, will be self liquidating; but there is that portion between, and the question is how that, would be cared for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: The general credit of the municipalities otherwise might be used for those portions which would not qualify under this legislation, but certainly I do not think we can widen the definition of "self-liquidating", and at the same time leave the measure a practicable piece of legislative machinery, especially having regard to the first remarks of my hon. friend. He spoke of the experience under the old housing act, which set up municipal authorities as lenders. But no municipality has come within that provision of that old act, because the provincial legislatures, from which the municipalities derive their powers, have not empowered them to do so. As I said in my remarks on the resolution the other day, we are dealing with institutions which are wholly the creatures of the provinces. We can deal with them only in such manner as will take that into account at all times. That is why we say in this bill that the project proposed by a municipality must have both the approval of the government and its guarantee of repayment. I do not think I can add anything to that.

Section 4 agreed to.

Under this section I should like to raise the point I brought up a few moments ago, the question 'of the rigidity with which the bill seems to be worded. A municipality can borrow at approximately

the rate of $3 per head of its population. A municipality, of say two hundred thousand people would be able to obtain a loan of about $600,000 for a project which it favoured. I do not see why the measure should be as rigid as that, and why there should not be in some section of the bill a clause providing a certain amount of flexibility where some worth while project is to be undertaken by a municipality, so that such municipality would be permitted a larger sum than is definitely provided in this measure. I think I can envisage many difficulties which might arise where a municipality of, say two hundred thousand people would require a loan of, let us say a million dollars for some good project. Under the existing bill that could not be done, and I would suggest that the minister take into serious consideration the question of developing some method so that, in a case such as I have mentioned, the amount stipulated in this bill might be increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: That clause is vital. I shall be perfectly frank with my hon. friend: I do not desire and the government does not desire to be placed in a position of even appearing to discriminate between the thousands of municipalities in this country. It is all very well for my hon. friend to rise in his place in the house to-day and say, " There might be a very good project in this municipality which ought to have a larger amount allowed, and there should be some flexibility." I can well imagine what would be the situation next year when some municipality had received more than another. There would be charges of political considerations, and of influence by hon. members, and all that sort of thing. This is a case in which the government and particularly the minister desire to operate within reasonable limits fixed by statute. I really wish to have this scheme worked on an economical basis and to have political considerations of preference here and there removed as far as it may be possible to do so. If in this legislation we make it possible for'one or two of our great cities to take larger amounts than their proportion of the whole population, I am afraid we shall seriously lower public confidence in the scheme. On the other hand, the exception which is provided in favour of the small municipalities is one which is, I think all hon. members will agree, very necessary in order to make it possible for small municipalities to take advantage of the legislation at all.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I would question the wisdom of and suggest to the minister that he reconsider the soundness of the principle which he enunciated here a few moments ago, of basing the limit of contribution on a ratio of population. The primary purpose of this bill as I understand it is to relieve unemployment or to create employment, and population in municipalities may have no relation in the world to the number of unemployed in any municipality. I think we know from experience that a much larger ratio of population is unemployed in the large centres than in the smaller centres of population. Surely that is so. I have listened in this chamber to members of the government explaining why we have this difficulty with the unemployed in British Columbia. In Vancouver they are congregated from all over Canada and particularly from all parts of British Columbia. I believe that every census which has been taken, including the census of the employment commission, indicates that the proportion, of unemployed to population is much greater in the larger centres than in the smaller. If the primary purpose of this bill is to provide employment, surely the basis on which a limitation of contribution or loan to any particular municipality should be fixed is the ratio of unemployed to the population in the particular place, rather than the population of a particular place to the whole population of Canada. I suggest that the minister might .-seriously consider that point.

speechtext: It is defined automatically. My hon. friend will note these words, "a loan not exceeding two hundred thousand dollars may be made to any municipality of whatever population." If we take the rule of thumb of $3 per head being the approximate amount, a municipality of 60,000 population would be entitled to only $180,000. Nevertheless, such a municipality will be able to obtain up to $200,000. By that method of computation, a municipality of 10,000 population would be able to get only $30,000; but if the other conditions are satisfactory, it will be able to obtain up to $200,000. The small municipality is defined by the break point of $200,000. I may tell my hon. friend that the figure in the first draft bill was $250,000, but it seemed to me that was too high a limit. Putting the break point at $200,000 means that municipalities with populations below 60,000 will be able to get $200,000. If we carried the other computation below that point, we would reach a figure which would be of no use at all.

This is an item that covers the whole administration of the department in question. Would the minister indicate in a few brief sentences the extent to which seasonal duties are maintained, and the extent to which the dumping duties are being operated, if at all, in his department? Would he give us at the same time a general idea regarding rebates? Unfortunately, as perhaps the minister knows, the auditor general's report, upon which we must rely, does not afford us any information subsequently to March 31, 1937, and inasmuch as we dealt with estimates in this house in 1937, we are, in the auditor general'ls report, dealing with something that has already been disposed of by the house. Hence I am emboldened to ask him now as to the general principles under
which the administration is now carrying on with respect to the matters to which I have referred.

The first matter to which the right hon. gentleman has referred is that of seasonal duties. Seasonal duties relate only to fruits and vegetables, and the system in force, as has been explained to the committee on several occasions, is that at certain times in the year, when the competition of United States fruits and vegetables is particularly serious, valuations for duty purposes are fixed by the Minister of National Revenue acting under the authority of an order in council that was passed some years ago. The values that are fixed are for the most part regional and for the most part, if not wholly, seasonal. The reason they are regional is that the season varies for different parts of Canada, and there are times when it would be very inconvenient and undesirable for United States fruits and vegetables to be shut out of certain parts of the dominion, even though it might be desirable for some action to be taken with respect to them in other parts of the country. For that reason the country, for administrative purposes, is divided into three districts: one comprising the four western provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba; another being the provinces of Ontario and Quebec; and the third, the maritime provinces. Sometimes values are fixed for the whole nine provinces, sometimes for the four western provinces and not for the others, sometimes for the two central provinces and not for the others, and so on, depending upon the supplies available in these districts. I believe the practice is well understood by the members of the house.
For a great many years there has been considerable dispute as to the application of fixed values and seasonal duties, and there have been many experiments looking to the best method of giving the fruit and vegetable growers of British Columbia, the central provinces and the maritime provinces reasonable protection without at the same time imposing undue hardship upon the importers, who must import large quantities of fruits and vegetables at all times. Since this government has been in office the Minister of Finance has stated on several occasions, as I too have done, that we carry on the protection of the fruit and Vegetable growers in as reasonable a way as we can by this method. The duties have been reduced as compared with those which were imposed by the previous administration. At the time of the negotiations with the United States, when the trade agreement was entered into, it was provided that advances on invoices
3486	COMMONS
Supply-National Revenue-Customs
should in no single instance be more than 80 per cent of the smallest advance made during the three previous years, and that has been carried out and more than carried out. In a number of instances they are not more than 60 per cent, and in one case not more than 40 per cent. Great care is given to the periods during which these values are imposed, and equal care is given to the amount of the advance that is regarded as proper.
The next subject on which the right hon. gentleman asked me to say a few words is that of dumping duties.
And their application.
Dumping duties date from about 1907.
And the principles are now well understood by importers and producers in Canada. The section which provides for the collection of special or dumping duty is section 6 of the customs tariff.
Much modified since it was first passed.

Yes; there have been amendments from time to time. But the principle which underlies the application and collection of dumping duties is this, that if the price at which the goods are purchased by the importer is less than the fair home market value, the difference between the invoice price and the fair home market value of the goods is collected in the way of special or dumping duty. But there is a provision that the amount collected shall in no case exceed 50 per cent of the value of the goods for duty purposes. There are various other provisions; that is the general principle. This applies only to goods of a class or kind produced in Canada.
That principle may be said to underlie the whole structure of dumping duties?
Yes.

The question I particularly wanted the minister to deal with was that which arises out of the determination of market value. It will be recalled that there was a reference before the tariff board-I saw something of it in the press; I have not had time to read the details-as to what price should be taken as the market price. That is, I buy in carload lots; someone else buys in smaller lots, and some other person buys in some other kind of lots. For the purpose of determining whether or not dumping duties should be paid, what is the governing price?

There is no problem more
difficult than that. The practice of the department for years has been this:	The trade
status of the importer is first ascertained. If the importer is a consumer, the value for duty is the fair home market price as paid by consumers in the country of origin. If the importer is a retailer, the value taken for duty purposes is the price paid in the principal markets of the country of origin by retailers. If the importer is a wholesaler, the value taken for duty purposes is the price paid by wholesalers in the country of origin. If the importer is a distributor-
Or jobber.

Well, I do not know the
difference between jobbers and wholesalers. I take them as meaning the same. But there is a trade status known as distributor, and distributors ordinarily are able to purchase goods at a lower price than wholesalers. If the importer is a distributor, the practice of the department has been to allow him to import at the distributor's price in the country of origin. In some instances there is no distributor in the country of origin; all the sales are to wholesalers, or perhaps to retailers or consumers. But the conditions are such that the merchandising of the goods through distributors in this country is the natural and proper way in which they should be merchandised. In that case we allow what are called distributors' discounts; there are a few such cases. We are authorized to do that under section 41 of the Customs Act.
I must say that the practice of the department has been challenged. A recent case before the tariff board has brought all the principles under review. A recent decision of the board-
In what case?
The insulating board case.
Has there been a decision?
Yes. The decision was that in that particular case the fair market value must be taken to be the price at which the greatest volume of goods moved into consumption in the country of origin.

Could be purchased by
anybody in that country?
The greatest volume.

I must say I do not know
what interpretation to put on the decision. If we divide the goods into five classes in that particular instance, in the country of origin perhaps 35 to 40 per cent are sold to wholesalers; those sales are greater than to any

other single class. The meaning of the decision probably is that we must take as the value for duty the price to the wholesalers in the country of origin because it is to that class of purchaser that the greatest volume of goods is sold. But it may be that the decision means something else entirely. It may be that the board had in mind two classes only, putting in one class the wholesalers and retail lumber dealers, who are almost wholesalers; they sell to contractors who in turn use the product in the building of houses. If that is what the tariff board meant, then we have wholesalers and retail dealers in one class. The sales to them hover around 50 per cent, and the application of the decision of the board may depend upon whether more or less than 50 per cent is sold to that class of wholesalers and lumber dealers.
Mr. BENNETT; Why would that follow?

I think the decision uses the term "wholesalers and jobbers," but possibly they mean wholesalers and dealers or jobbers and dealers. The reason given in the decision is that, more than half of the output being sold to these classes of purchasers, they constitute the principal market in the country of origin; and when section 35 refers to the sale in the principal markets of the country of origin, it means to the largest class of purchasers. If we adopt that principle for value in the future, it will make some change in the practice of the department. But I am glad to say that the tariff board was very careful to point out that they were not laying down a general principle but simply saying that in that particular instance they think the "fair home market value in the principal markets" means the price at which the greatest volume of goods moves into consumption.

I am obliged to the minister. Some people resident in the constituency I have the honour to represent were interested in a motion which has been pending in this house since February 16 in connection with the application of the customs tariff by the officers and clerks of the Department of National Revenue. I was not aware that the insulating board case had been decided until the minister was good enough to say so. The effect of that decision I understand to be that the market price which has to be considered in determining whether or not dumping duty should be applied is the price at which the largest volume of that commodity was being sold in that country and could be purchased by anyone who qualified as a purchaser. That would be correct?
Yes; that is it exactly.

Then it would seem to me that if this rule were applied reasonably, it would prevent the inquiries that have been going on as to whether John Smith was just a casual purchaser or whether he was a purchaser of ten gross or of a thousand gross, we will say, of a given commodity. The only matter that should be inquired into when I lodge my invoice with the department is whether or not I actually could buy that commodity in the market of origin at the price indicated.

Buyers in the same
category.

No; that is what I want to get away from. That is what I want to find out about, because that is the matter about which there has been so much difficulty.
I buy goods in New York to-morrow; I come to the customs house here and hand in my invoice showing that I bought them at a store on Broadway, and showing what I paid for them. The department says, "We want dumping duty from you, Mr. Bennett." I say, "You are not entitled to dumping duty, because I bought those goods at the price at which anybody else could buy them in that store on Broadway, and therefore the section does not apply." That is the contention I want to put fairly up to the minister, as it is put up to me by those who are interested in the matter in the part of the country in which I live.
Have I made myself clear? I purchase a bill of goods in a store in New York; I get my invoice and hand it in here, and I am told, "Oh, no, you cannot have that at that rate; you have to pay dumping duty." But I say, "I am not going to pay dumping duty; you have no right to ask me for it." Then the official says. "Let us see. Are you a retailer or a consumer, or what are you?" I say, "That is none of your business. I bought these goods, and anybody else could buy them in that community for exactly the same price. Therefore I have come within the statute; that is the market price at which those goods can be bought in that community." I am talking about the legislation as it now stands; I am not saying what it might be. That is the position taken by those who are keenly and deeply interested. They say, "This statute does not allow them to do this; this statute does not permit officials to make inquiries," and it will be remembered that the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross), in his resolution of February 16, dealt with that particular phase of the matter, and in a moment I am going to say something about another phase of it.
