How do we find ourselves, in the administration of this act, authorized to take dumping duties from an importer when he has bought his goods at a price at which, Smith, Jones and Brown in New York can buy them on the same day in the same store? Surely we cannot take a dumping duty in that case; yet I know of instances that have been brought to my attention in which the department have been saying, "You have to pay dumping duty, because you are not the same type and class of purchaser as the other person who bought them in New York." I say that is not your business; if these men can walk into a store in New York and buy those goods at the same price. I buy them for that price; it is on my invoice, and 1 pay my duty on that price. In that statute there is no power given to enable the department to exact a dumping duty from me.
I am putting this to the minister because it is not a conjectural case; it is the position that is put to me, that the law does not authorize it. I apologize for taking time on it; but it is a vital matter to people who find themselves coming across the border, who are not within the exemption, and who are paying duty from day to day. I remember how bitter was the complaint in one instance, and on inquiry I found that this citizen who was importing these goods was paying exactly the price that Smith, Jones and Brown would pay for these goods in that store in New York, although it may be said that Smith, Brown and Jones bought in larger volume than my friend did. But I say, under the law as it stands, that is not the concern of the department. They have one question to decide; that is whether I bought these goods honestly and openly for what was the market price of those goods in that city, and "market price" means the price at which the goods could be marketed by the seller to a buyer in that city. Have I made myself clear?

The right hon. gentleman has made himself perfectly clear, and I agree as to the importance of the question he has raised. I am not at all sure just what the act does authorize the department to do, but I am of a contrary opinion to the right hon. gentleman.
Perhaps if the minister has the section before him, he might read it in order that I might better follow his observations.

It is section 35. Needless to say, I have given a great deal of thought to this very matter. I do not know whether the right hon. gentleman is expressing these views as his own or whether he is putting [Mr. Bennett.J
forth what might be a reasonable interpretation of the act and suggesting that he would like me to give my views on it. I do not agree with that construction of the act. When the right hon, gentleman goes into a store in New York and buys goods which he brings to the border, or which he has sent to him, we are confronted with the duty of ascertaining whether he has paid the fair market value of the goods when sold for home consumption in the principal markets of the country of origin, which would be the United States.
That is why I selected New York.

In order to give a reasonable and workable interpretation of that section, we must take sales under substantially similar conditions to purchasers in the United States. I think that is the only reasonable interpretation which can 'be placed on the act. We ask ourselves: What do United States purchasers pay for those goods when they go into a store in New York and buy them?
Mr, BENNETT: In my illustration they went into that store that day, bought these goods and paid the price I paid for them. The minister perhaps did not follow me. I bought my goods in New York. Brown, Smith and Jones bought their goods in New York in the same store on the same day, and paid for them x price. I paid the same x price. It is true that the price which Jones, Smith and Brown paid was a price which they paid because they bought in large volume in the United States, but it is also true that I was given that same price; and having been given that price, that was the market price in that city to United States citizens for those goods.
Mr. ILSLEY': Yes, but not to United States citizens generally.
Where is there anything like that in the act?
It does not say it, but I say the section must be interpreted in that way; otherwise it is entirely unworkable.
No.
I think it is.

Section 35 states:
1.	Whenever any duty ad valorem is imposed on any goods imported into Canada, the value for duty shall be the fair market value thereof, when sold for home consumption, in the principal markets of the country whence and at the time when the same were exported directly to Canada.
2.	In the case of importations of goods the manufacture or produce of a foreign country,

Supply-
-National Revenue-Customs
the currency of which is substantially depreciated, the value for duty shall not be less than the value that would be placed on similar (roods manufactured or produced in Great Britain and imported from that country, if such similar goods are made or produced there.
3.	If similar goods are not made or produced in Great Britain, the value for duty shall not be less than the value of similar goods made or produced in any European country the currency of which is not substantially depreciated.
4.	The minister may determine the value of such goods, and the value so determined shall, until otherwise provided, be the value upon which the duty on such goods shall be computed and levied under regulations prescribed by the minister.
The first subsection, is the one in which we are interested; that is:
Whenever any duty ad valorem is imposed on any goods imported into Canada, the value for duty shall be the fair market value thereof, when sold for home consumption, in the principal markets of the country whence and at the time when the same were exported directly to Canada.
This was brought to my attention by an importer, and as a matter of fact I did turn up this section. I have no excuse to give him when he tells me that they gave him a price in New York which was the same price that Jones and Smith and Brown paid for those goods.
What was the status of the sellers? Were they manufacturers or wholesalers?

They were wholesalers. There are two lines of cases, both of which have been presented to me, but for the sake of this discussion I had better deal with the wholesaler rather than the manufacturer. I will deal with the manufactured goods in another way. I am not talking about what the statute should say; I am talking of what it does say. The minister appreciates that point. Jones and Smith and Brown were ahead of me in that store on Broadway, that wholesale shop. They bought an invoice of goods. I was there; I saw their invoices, and I said to them, "Is this the price you paid without discount or anything else, buying these goods in the United States"? And they answered, "Yes, that is what we paid." 'fit is not a fire sale; it is a regular sale by this wholesaler"? "Yes." I say to the clerk, " I want an invoice of ten dozen of these' goods." "Well, the price should be a little higher than that, should it not '? he will probably say to me; " you are going to use them here"? That has been said to me. I sav, "No; I am taking them out of this country." "Well, then, you can have the same price as is paid by the Americans who
use them in this country." It is within the knowledge of the minister that sometimes they offer to shade the price, but we are not talking about shading the price. They give me my invoice for exactly the same price. My contention is that when my goods reach this city and I go down to the long room with my invoice, as the law now stands there is no power given to the Dominion of Canada to take any more money from me by way of duty than upon the computation of the price which is in that invoice, because it is established that three people bought those goods at the same price for use and consumption in the United States.
Resale. Undoubtedly, in the case put, the Americans bought the goods for re-sale. They were retailers buying from a wholesaler.

They come within this,
" the fair market price for home consumption," at any rate.
Oh, well, yes.

It may be that cases might arise which necessitate a change in the law; but just where an official of this country is given a right to say to me or to my friends, "Although you 'bought your goods at the same price as that which Jones and Smith and Brown paid for theirs, and although they are using theirs in the United States and you have taken yours to Canada, I shall ask you to pay a dumping duty or an increased duty on them," I do not know; I say I cannot find it in the four corners of the statute. If it is desired to put it there, it should be put there. I take it that that was what was in the mind of the mover of the resolution with respect to this matter. The minister asks me my opinion with respect to it. I am bound to say that when I read the discussion which took place in the newspapers with respect to insulating board I was rather surprised. I could not think that there is anything in the statute which permits officials of the department to go beyond the language of the act. There is nothing there about volume or substantial conditions or anything else; it is the fair market price paid by consumers or purchasers in that country.
Let me now take the retail case, which brings it nearer home. I have known, as most hon. members of this committee have, people who sometimes secure bargains, very great bargains, on a bargain day in one of the large New York stores. My contention is that, under the law as it stands, there is no authority in this country to take from me a larger duty than the invoice calls for, because

Supply-National Revenue-Customs
that was a bargain sale that everybody could avail themselves of, and it was a retail sale. That is the position which I hope I have made perfectly clear to the minister. I am 'bound to say I believe that if it is desired to apply some other principle, the statute should be amended, because I do not believe that, under the terms of the statute as it stands, that power is there. That is the submission I have to make.

It would probably be desirable to have the act clarified in some way, because the dispute which took place over insulating board showed that the problem was very difficult, and I do not know whether the reasons given by the department for the practice were altogether valid or sound.
I think it is only fair to say that the practice is nothing new; it did not arise since the minister took office.

I think the practice of the
department is authorized by the section. I shall try to explain why I think so, although I may not meet the right hon. gentleman point by point.
The duty of our appraisers is to "ascertain, estimate and appraise"-those are the words -the fair market value of the goods when sold for home consumption, and so on. Now there will be several fair market values of those goods in the country of origin.
And I say that Canadians can always take the lowest.

Yes; they will likely get
the lowest, because the sale will be made in that way and there will not be any undesirable consequences to the sellers; that is the reason they will get the lowest. But sometimes there will be three levels, each of which is the fair market value of the goods when sold for home consumption, depending upon what? Upon the status or class of the purchaser. That is what it depends upon.

Yes; but the statute
does not say so.

As yet I am a thousand
miles from what the statute says. I am simply stating what the facts are. The facts are that, taking that area in the United States in which he has bought the goods he will find certainly two and probably three price levels ordinarily prevalent. If the man is a consumer, he will find he has to pay so much for the hat or whatever it is; if he is a retailer, he will have to pay a lower price; and if he is a wholesaler, he need only pay still less.

And if I am fortunate
enough to buy at the lowest of the three prices, I am penalized for doing so.
Mr. ILSLE1 :	The right hon. gentleman
is not logical there. He has branched off on to a matter of policy when we are discussing at the moment a question of law, and law only. We can reach the question of policy later. What I am saying is that in the case I have put there are three levels of prices. How are our officers going to determine what is the fair home market value of these goods for customs purposes? Well, there is only one way if the section is to be operated at all, and that is to consider what class the purchaser was in; -what his status was in purchasing. We have to consider what the price would be under similar conditions, that is, the fair home market value so far as that particular instance is concerned.
That is not what the statute says.

That is a reasonable interpretation to place upon the statute, just as reasonable as the right hon. gentleman's interpretation. Why does the right hon. gentleman say that the price he paid as a consumer buying from a wholesaler was the fair home market value, when the fair home market value to consumers, to people in the same position as he, was so much higher? It is our duty to find out how much higher that price is. When we find out how much they are paying, then we know what is the fair home market value. That is the reason why that rule has been adopted by the department. The right hon. gentleman says that he is penalized because he buys these articles. Of course he is because that is the principle of the dumping clause. It has been debated for thirty years whether it is fair to penalize buyers for buying too low in a foreign country. The principle is settled, and observations of that kind are off the track.
The minister will observe that I did not make any objection to the dumping clause. I have supported it too many times. Perhaps the hon. gentleman was not always as warm in his support as I was.
I am not warm about it; I am simply arguing a legal point.

I said he was not as warm in his support of the dumping duty as I have been. The principle of the dumping duty is not quite as the hon. gentleman states. The principle of the dumping duty was to protect us against surplus products being dumped on our market at prices that bore no relation to

Supply-National Revenue-Customs
the market value. I could give case after case. Here is a factory which sells 80 per cent of its production at home. It may be that in cider to keep the factory going at full time, the remaining 20 per cent of the production is sold at a 30 per cent discount under what it is being sold for in the United States. I think Mr. Fielding was the father of the dumping duty. I remember reading his speech about it and thinking it was a very fair statement of the situation.
Let me give another illustration. There is a great sale going on in New York, to last all this week. I go down there, and as one of a million other people I buy certain goods at a tremendously low price. I cannot find any authority in the statute that will enable this government or the officials of this department to charge any rate of duty that may be called a dumping duty with respect to those goods. The price I paid was the fair market price. Tou say, "That is not the fact." Of course you say it is not the fact. It is the old story that was dealt with by the price spreads committee. It is a matter of selling goods to clear them out and thereby make it difficult for the smaller retailer to continue in business. I am only pointing out to the minister that however laudable it may be-he will observe I have been careful not to say it was not-there is no provision in the statute that enables this to be done. These are not importers I am talking about; these are people who went across the line and bought goods in a store on Fifth avenue or Broadway. But they found they could not get the goods through on the invoice price because they were told it was a bargain sale. The fact is that this was the price at which anyone could buy them.

The right hon. gentleman is talking about a purely theoretical case. It would be news to me if we had ever attempted to collect a dumping duty from a consumer because of the price he paid in the country of origin.
I will admit he did not consume them all.

The right hon. gentleman
spoke about going down to a bargain sale and being asked to pay a dumping duty. That has never happened in the history of the department.

Not as against an individual consumer, but I am talking about a consumer who purchases more than his own requirements. Some he gives away, and he lets somebody else reimburse him in connection with some of the rest. I must say
that I do not believe the department has any right under that statute to charge any more than the invoice price.

products has been mentioned during the course of this discussion, and possibly the minister might be in position to give the committee further details in this connection.

Well then, I think there has been an erroneous impression spread throughout Ontario, by the premier of the province stating that in cases where be was sure there was fraud and refused to settle succession duty taxes, he received absolutely no cooperation from the department at Ottawa.
Well, I have stated what the facts are.
Thank you.

Through the mounted police.

I am a little
troubled by the phrase "to be disbursed by and accounted for to it for customs-excise and income tax secret investigation services." Should not that be "accounted for by it"?
It means accounted for to the Department of National Revenue.

The Department of National Revenue tells the Department of Justice to whom to pay the amounts. That is what is meant by the words "accounted for to it." The amounts are paid by the Department of Justice at the request of the Department of National Revenue. The Department of Justice must be furnished with the names of the persons and the reasons for payment.
